title: A Queen Refuses the King
overview: At a huge Persian royal party, Queen Vashti refuses the king's order to show herself to his guests, and his alarmed advisers have her removed, which opens the way for the story of Esther.

parts.label: An empire on display (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: The king is usually identified with Xerxes I of Persia, who ruled a vast empire stretching from India to Cush, the land along the upper Nile. The 180 days were probably a long season of showing off his wealth to leaders from many provinces, not a single nonstop meal.

parts.label: A week of feasting (vv. 5-8)
parts.note: The rich fabrics, gold couches and stone floors stress how lavish the court was, and digs at Susa have uncovered a great columned hall that fits this setting. Guests could drink as much or as little as they liked, with no one forcing them.

parts.label: Vashti says no (vv. 9-12)
parts.note: Men and women feasted separately, as was the custom, and on the last day the king, merry with wine, ordered the queen brought out so his guests could look at her beauty. The text never says why or how she refused, though many readers think she would not be put on display before a room of drinking men.

parts.label: The advisers react (vv. 13-18)
parts.note: The king turns to his seven highest nobles, and Memucan blows one refusal up into a threat to every husband in the empire. Many readers see the story gently mocking these powerful men and their fear of their own wives.

parts.label: A decree that cannot change (vv. 19-22)
parts.note: Vashti is banned from the king's presence by a Persian law that cannot be undone, an idea that matters later in the book, and this leaves the queen's place open for Esther. Many readers take the order sent out in every language, telling men to rule their homes, as the story poking fun at a king trying to command respect by decree.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether Vashti is a woman of dignity rightly refusing to be made a spectacle or a wife wrongly defying her husband, and on how far the chapter is meant as satire of the Persian court.
think: Why do you think one person's refusal can feel so threatening to people who hold a great deal of power?
